analysis.one_liner: Creates a government jobs and training fund for the unemployed, paid for by a small tax on stock and futures trades.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would fund jobs for the long-term unemployed through a 0.25% tax on securities trades, died in committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would create a national trust fund to pay for direct public jobs and job training in communities with high unemployment. The fund would be financed by a new tax of 0.25% on stock, bond, and futures trades, paid by the trading facilities that handle them. It also would require that a quarter of the seats on state and local workforce boards go to minority-serving community organizations, and it would convene a national conference on unemployment. The bill was referred to two House committees and a subcommittee, where it stayed until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Long-term unemployed and low-income workers, especially in distressed communities: the bill funds jobs repairing schools and parks, fighting blight, and staffing child care and food programs, with prevailing-wage rules and a requirement that most money go to wages and benefits. Disadvantaged youth get job and training programs, and minority-serving community organizations gain seats on workforce boards. Job training participants could receive stipends.

how_it_helps.text: Creates Employment Opportunity Grants to states, cities, counties, and tribes for jobs in distressed communities — repairing schools and parks, restoring vacant properties, expanding food programs, and staffing Head Start and child care — whenever the Fed Chairman determines the economy is not at full employment [S2][S3].

Requires grant recipients to spend at least 80% of project funding on wages, benefits, and support services like child care, pay at least 35% of workers from targeted disadvantaged groups, follow prevailing-wage rules on construction, and guarantee 12-month jobs of at least 30 hours a week [S3].
Requires workers hired to be either long-term unemployed (26 weeks or more) or low-income members of targeted groups, and bars grant-funded jobs from displacing existing or furloughed employees [S3].
Finances the program with a 0.25% tax on securities transactions, paid by the trading facility on which each transaction occurs, rather than by general revenue [S3].
Requires that at least 25% of the chief executives on state and local workforce investment boards come from minority-serving, community-based organizations [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Traders, brokerages, and other financial market participants, through a 0.25% tax on every covered stock, bond, and futures transaction; trading facilities would remit the tax, and part of the cost could be passed to investors through higher trading costs [S3].

drawbacks.text: The new tax would apply to every covered securities and futures transaction, and while it is remitted by trading facilities, some or all of the cost would likely be passed through to the investors and savers making the trades [S3].

Funding is not guaranteed: deposits into the trust fund are subject to the availability of appropriations, grants flow only if the Federal Reserve Chairman determines the economy is below full employment, and jobs funded are temporary, with a minimum of 12 months and no commitment afterward [S3].

Job placements are tightly targeted — 35% must go to workers unemployed at least 30 days who are low-income members of targeted groups, or other workers with 26 weeks of unemployment — which focuses aid narrowly but excludes other unemployed people [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would put wages into the hands of long-term unemployed and low-income people in high-poverty areas while requiring most spending to go to pay and benefits, and it uses the financial transaction tax rather than general borrowing to pay for it. The real trade-offs are that the tax adds a small cost to every securities trade that may reach ordinary investors, the jobs are temporary, and the trigger depends on the Federal Reserve Chairman's judgment of full employment. On balance the benefits are targeted at people with the least income and the costs fall on the most active trading.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Education and the Workforce and Ways and Means committees in 2013, then on to a workforce subcommittee, and no committee ever acted on it, so it never reached the House floor before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John Conyers Jr. introduced the bill on February 27, 2013, joined by 15 Democratic cosponsors [S1][S4].

It was referred to both the Committee on Education and the Workforce and the Committee on Ways and Means, and on April 23, 2013 was referred to the Subcommittee on Higher Education and Workforce Training [S5].
No further action was taken after that referral; the bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote and died when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Securities and futures trading firms benefit from having never paid the 0.25% transaction tax the bill would have imposed, and no public jobs or training fund was created for the unemployed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Securities trading firms, which avoided the tax

for.name: Rep. John Conyers Jr.
for.role: Sponsor; Dean of the House, Representative from Michigan
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on it [S1][S5].

for.name: 15 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all 15 cosponsors were Democrats, including Reps. Cummings, Ellison, Lee, Grijalva, and Fudge [S3][S4].

against.name: House Education and the Workforce Committee
against.role: Committee of primary referral (Chair: Rep. John Kline, R-MN)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and took no action; it was sent to the Subcommittee on Higher Education and Workforce Training in April 2013 and never received a markup or vote [S5].

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Second committee of referral (Chair: Rep. Dave Camp, R-MI)
against.what_they_did: Received the tax title of the bill by referral and took no action on it for the life of the bill [S5].

sides.party_line_note: All 16 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican supported it; the Republican-controlled committees to which it was referred took no action [S3][S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would impose a 0.25% tax on every covered securities and futures transaction, remitted by the trading facility, reducing trading industry revenue; it died, so no tax was ever collected. The tax would have been the funding source for jobs and training for the unemployed [S3].
They would gain guaranteed seats on state and local workforce boards and could act as grant-funded employers or service providers for the new jobs programs [S2][S3].

industries.industry: State and local governments and Indian tribes
industries.note: They would receive Employment Opportunity Grants to fund public jobs repairing schools, parks, and vacant properties and staffing child care and food programs in distressed communities [S2][S3].
Grant-funded construction must pay prevailing wages, and grant-funded workers could not be placed where a union contract covers the same work without union consent, protecting union standards [S3].
